units.title: The .NET Framework era
units.blurb: Why Microsoft built .NET, how Framework grew from generics to async, and why 4.8 is the last version yet still powers plugins for older Revit and AutoCAD.

lessons.title: Why .NET was born
lessons.sub: Windows programs before 2002 and what went wrong

cards.title: Writing Windows apps in the 90s
cards.body:
Serious apps were written in C++ against the raw Win32 API. Quick forms were built in Visual Basic 6. Components written in different languages talked to each other through COM.

It worked, but it hurt: manual memory management, leaks and crashes. Installing one app could break another.

cards.title: DLL hell
cards.body:
Apps shared DLLs in a system folder. A new app would install its own version of a library over the old one, and an older app would stop starting.

People called this DLL hell.

cards.q: What is DLL hell?
options: One app replaces a shared library with its own version and breaks other apps
Too many DLLs in an app folder
cards.explain: .NET fixed this with versioned, strong-named assemblies, and later by letting each app carry its own dependencies.

cards.title: Meanwhile, there was Java
cards.body:
Since 1995 Java had promised "write once, run anywhere". Code compiles to bytecode, a virtual machine runs it, and a garbage collector cleans up memory.

Microsoft built its own Java (J++), added Windows-only extensions and lost a lawsuit to Sun. It needed a platform of its own.

cards.title: 2002: .NET Framework 1.0
cards.body:
The ideas are close to Java, but built for Windows and for many languages:

CLR: the runtime. JIT, garbage collection, type safety.
BCL: a large standard library.
C#: a new language. Its lead designer is Anders Hejlsberg, who had already created Turbo Pascal and Delphi.
cards.deep: C# and the CLI (Common Language Infrastructure) were standardized at ECMA (ECMA-334 and ECMA-335) back in 2001-2002. That let others build their own implementation, and that is how Mono appeared.

cards.task: Find the year .NET Framework 1.0 came out and see which systems it ran on.

cards.q: Match each part of .NET to its role
pairs: A new language for the platform
The old way to connect components

cards.q: Which problems did .NET solve? Select all that apply.
options: Different languages could not easily work together
Apps did not run on Linux
cards.explain: For its first 14 years, official .NET ran only on Windows. Linux came later, first through Mono.

cards.q: Who is the lead designer of C#?
cards.explain: Gosling created Java, and Stroustrup created C++.

lessons.title: Framework grows up
lessons.sub: Generics, WPF, LINQ, async, version by version

cards.title: Every version was a big step
cards.body: Framework and C# grew together. Almost every release brought something you can hardly imagine C# without today.

cards.title: 2005, 2.0: generics
cards.body: List<int> instead of ArrayList: the compiler checks the type, and numbers are not boxed into objects. Generics live in the CLR itself, not just in the language. Java does it differently.

cards.title: 2006-2007: 3.0 and 3.5
cards.body:
3.0: WPF (a new XAML-based UI), WCF (network services), Workflow Foundation.

3.5 and C# 3.0: LINQ, lambdas, var, extension methods. Queries over collections and databases, written in plain C#.

cards.title: 2010-2012: 4.0 and 4.5
cards.body:
4.0: the Task Parallel Library, TPL (Task, Parallel.For), and dynamic.

4.5 and C# 5: async and await. Asynchronous code that reads like ordinary code.

cards.task: Find the year async and await arrived in C#.

cards.q: Put these in chronological order
cards.explain: Each feature built on the ones before it: LINQ needs generics and lambdas, and async needs Task.

cards.q: Match each version to its headline feature
How do .NET generics differ from Java generics?
options: They exist in the runtime itself: List<int> stores real ints with no boxing
cards.explain: Java erases generics at compile time, so List<Integer> stores objects.

cards.q: What made async/await possible?
cards.explain: await waits on a task. Task came first, and two years later C# got a convenient syntax for it.

lessons.title: Framework 4.8: the end of the road
lessons.sub: Why it stopped evolving and why you still need it

cards.title: Framework is part of Windows
cards.body:
.NET Framework is installed once per system and shared by everyone. Version 4.x replaces the previous 4.x in place: install 4.8, and every app built for 4.5 now runs on 4.8.

So any change in behavior risks breaking thousands of other people's apps. Serious changes became almost impossible.

cards.q: Why is Framework so hard to evolve?
options: One shared copy for the whole system: a change can break every installed app
cards.explain: Modern .NET versions install side by side, and each app picks its own.

cards.title: 2019: the last major version
cards.body:
.NET Framework 4.8 shipped in 2019, and 4.8.1 added ARM64 support in 2022. No new features are coming, only security fixes.

It is supported for as long as the Windows version it ships with. So "legacy" does not mean "dead".

cards.task: Find the year .NET Framework 4.8 came out. What else shipped that year?

cards.title: Why you still need it: plugins
cards.body:
A plugin is a DLL that a host app loads into its own process. That means the plugin runs on whatever runtime the host runs on.

Revit 2024 and AutoCAD 2024 run on .NET Framework 4.8, so their plugins must target Framework 4.8 too. Revit and AutoCAD 2025 moved to .NET 8.

cards.q: A Revit 2024 plugin is built for net8.0. What happens?
options: Revit will not load it: Revit 2024 runs on .NET Framework 4.8
cards.explain: The host decides the runtime. The plugin adapts to the host, not the other way around.

cards.q: What is true about .NET Framework 4.8? Select all that apply.
options: It will get new C# versions and new APIs
Plugins for older Revit and AutoCAD need it
cards.explain: Officially, Framework supports C# up to 7.3. Many newer language features still compile for it, but it will never get new APIs.

cards.q: A plugin project for Revit 2024
cards.explain: net48 is how a project names .NET Framework 4.8.

cards.q: Match each item to what it means

cards.task: Walk through the key Framework years: 2002, 2005, 2007, 2012 and 2019.

cards.q: Put these in chronological order
Which 90s problem did .NET solve with versioned assemblies?
cards.explain: An assembly knows its version, and an app asks for the one it needs.

cards.q: Why will Framework 4.8 get no new APIs?
options: It is shared by all of Windows and updated in place, so changing it is risky, and development moved to the new .NET
cards.explain: Only modern .NET gets new features.

cards.q: Where is Framework 4.8 still needed today? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Revit 2025 is already on .NET 8, and Framework does not run on Linux.

cards.q: Match each year to what it brought
A plugin runs on the runtime of...
options: whatever was installed last on the system
cards.explain: A plugin lives in the host's process, so it lives in the host's runtime too.

cards.q: A plugin for AutoCAD 2024
cards.explain: AutoCAD 2024, like Revit 2024, runs on Framework 4.8.

units.title: Mono, Unity and Xamarin
units.blurb: An open implementation of the ECMA standard, C# in Unity (Mono, IL2CPP, the road to CoreCLR) and on phones: Xamarin and MAUI.

lessons.title: Mono: .NET without Microsoft
lessons.sub: How C# reached Linux long before .NET Core

cards.title: An open standard invites new implementations
cards.body:
Microsoft submitted the C# and CLI specs to ECMA as a standard. That meant anyone could write their own runtime from the spec.

Miguel de Icaza and his company Ximian did exactly that: in 2004 they released Mono 1.0, .NET for Linux.

cards.task: Find the year Mono 1.0 came out and see where you could now run C#.

cards.q: How could Mono be built without Microsoft's source code?
options: C# and the CLI are described in an open ECMA standard
Mono is just a renamed Framework
cards.explain: It is an independent implementation of an open spec.

cards.title: Mono's journey
cards.body:
Novell bought Ximian (2003). In 2011 Novell laid off the team, and they founded Xamarin: C# for iOS and Android, built on Mono. In 2016 Microsoft bought Xamarin.

In 2024 Microsoft handed the Mono project over to the WineHQ community. The Mono runtime also lives on inside modern .NET, for mobile platforms and WebAssembly.

cards.q: Put Mono's journey in order
cards.explain: Mono started in 2001, Novell bought Ximian in 2003, Xamarin was founded in 2011, Microsoft bought it in 2016, and WineHQ took over in 2024.

cards.q: Where did Mono run? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Linux and macOS were the whole point. Unity also embedded it in its engine.

cards.q: Match each name to what it is
What does the Mono runtime do inside modern .NET today?
options: Runs .NET on mobile platforms and in WebAssembly
cards.explain: It is small, so it fits well where CoreCLR is too heavy.

lessons.title: Unity and its C#
lessons.sub: Mono inside the engine, IL2CPP and the road to CoreCLR

cards.title: Engine in C++, scripts in C#
cards.body:
Unity itself is written in C++. Game logic, though, is written in C#: the engine embeds a runtime and calls your scripts.

In 2005 that runtime was Mono, the only .NET that ran on the Mac, where Unity was born.

cards.task: Find the year Unity 1.0 came out.

cards.title: Years on old Mono
cards.body: For a long time Unity shipped an old Mono with roughly .NET 3.5-level features. Only in 2018 did it move to a newer Mono with the .NET 4.x API and .NET Standard 2.0. Since Unity 2021.2 it supports .NET Standard 2.1.

cards.title: IL2CPP
cards.body: On iOS, consoles and WebGL, JIT is either forbidden or impossible. So Unity built IL2CPP: CIL bytecode is translated to C++, which is then compiled to machine code ahead of time.
cards.deep: Because everything is compiled ahead of time, IL2CPP has limits: generating code at run time (Reflection.Emit) is not supported, and generic instantiations the compiler never saw may be missing. It is the same class of problems as Native AOT in modern .NET.

cards.q: Why did Unity build IL2CPP?
options: iOS, consoles and WebGL do not allow JIT, so machine code must exist ahead of time
cards.explain: Same motive as Native AOT: no JIT, so compile everything before launch.

cards.title: Next up: CoreCLR
cards.body: In 2022 Unity announced a move to CoreCLR, the same runtime modern .NET uses. That means better speed and newer C# and libraries. The move is happening step by step.

cards.q: What is true about Unity? Select all that apply.
options: The engine itself is written in C++
C# scripts run on embedded Mono or IL2CPP
Unity ran on CoreCLR from day one
cards.explain: CoreCLR is Unity's future, not its past.

cards.q: Match each term to its role in Unity
A library uses Reflection.Emit to generate code on the fly. Where will it break?
options: In a Unity build using IL2CPP
In the Unity editor on Mono
cards.explain: Without a JIT, there is nothing to run code generated on the fly.

cards.title: Xamarin: C# for iOS and Android
cards.body:
Xamarin (2011) let you write mobile apps in C# and share code between iOS and Android. At first it cost money, and quite a lot of it.

In 2016 Microsoft bought Xamarin and made it free.

cards.task: Find the year Microsoft bought Xamarin. What else big happened that year?

cards.title: Xamarin.Forms → .NET MAUI
cards.body:
Xamarin.Forms gave you one XAML UI for every platform. In 2022 it was replaced by .NET MAUI: the same approach, but on modern .NET, plus Windows and macOS.

Xamarin support ended in May 2024.

cards.title: Native controls vs drawing it yourself
cards.body:
MAUI turns your button into a real iOS or Android button: native controls. It looks and feels native, but differs slightly on each platform.

Avalonia draws everything itself, like a game: pixel-identical everywhere. More on that in the Avalonia course.

cards.q: How does MAUI's approach differ from Avalonia's?
options: MAUI uses the platform's native controls, Avalonia draws the UI itself
cards.explain: Hence the trade-off: MAUI looks native, Avalonia looks the same everywhere.

cards.q: Put these in chronological order
Match each technology to what it is
pairs: C# on iOS and Android, built on Mono

cards.q: What is true? Select all that apply.
options: MAUI is the new version of WPF
cards.explain: WPF is a separate, Windows-only technology.

cards.task: Walk through the years: Mono (2004), Unity (2005), Xamarin (2011) and the Xamarin acquisition (2016).

cards.q: Why did Unity pick Mono over .NET Framework in 2005?
options: Unity was born on the Mac, and Framework ran only on Windows
cards.explain: Microsoft had no cross-platform .NET back then.

cards.q: A game is built for iPhone. How does Unity run the C#?
options: IL2CPP: the code is translated to C++ and machine code ahead of time
cards.explain: JIT is not allowed on iOS.

cards.q: What did Microsoft do in 2016? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Framework is still supported today.

cards.q: Put these in chronological order
Match each term to what it is
Where is Unity heading?
options: To CoreCLR, the runtime of modern .NET
cards.explain: Announced in 2022, the move is happening step by step.

cards.q: What if there had been no ECMA standards?
options: Mono, and with it Unity and Xamarin, would have been much harder to build
cards.explain: The open spec is what the whole "other" branch of .NET grew from.

units.title: Open source, .NET Core and .NET Standard
units.blurb: Open source, a new cross-platform .NET, the standard as an API contract, and why 2.1 is in Unity and .NET 10 but not in Framework. Plus multi-targeting.

cards.title: A U-turn
cards.body:
In the early 2000s Microsoft called open source a threat. In 2014, under new CEO Satya Nadella, it open-sourced .NET.

The reason was practical: servers increasingly ran Linux, and a Windows-only platform was losing to Java, Node.js and Go.

cards.title: What was opened
cards.body:
Roslyn: the C# and VB compiler, written in C# itself. Analyzers and IDE hints use its API.

.NET Foundation: an independent foundation for open-source projects.

.NET Core: a new cross-platform .NET under the MIT license, developed in the open on GitHub.

cards.task: Find the year Microsoft open-sourced .NET.

cards.q: What is Roslyn?
options: The C# and VB compiler with an open API, written in C#
cards.explain: Analyzers, refactorings and source generators all run on Roslyn.

cards.q: What does the MIT license allow?
options: You can use, change and sell the code as long as you keep the copyright notice
You can only read the code
You can use it only in non-commercial projects
cards.explain: It is one of the most permissive licenses around.

cards.q: Why did Microsoft open up .NET? Select all that apply.
options: Servers and clouds ran Linux at scale
Competitors (Java, Node.js, Go) were open and cross-platform
The community can send in fixes
It ran out of money for development
cards.explain: Today a noticeable share of changes in dotnet/runtime comes from people outside Microsoft.

cards.q: Match each name to what it is
Where can you read the source of List<T> or the garbage collector today?
options: In the open dotnet repos on GitHub
cards.explain: You can even step through it in a debugger: Source Link fetches the sources for you.

cards.title: Not a new Framework version, but a new .NET
cards.body: Framework could not be changed: all of Windows shares it. So .NET Core was built as a separate platform. The team kept the best parts, rewrote a lot and dropped the rest.

cards.title: What changed
cards.body:
Cross-platform: Windows, Linux, macOS.
Side-by-side versions: .NET 6, 8 and 10 live on one machine, and each app uses its own.
Self-contained: you can ship the runtime with your app.
The dotnet command: dotnet new, dotnet build, dotnet run.
Speed: release after release, .NET Core gets noticeably faster than Framework.

cards.task: Follow the path of .NET Core: 1.0 (2016), 2.0 (2017) and 3.x (2019).

cards.title: What was left behind
cards.body:
Some parts of Framework never made it into Core:

AppDomain (isolation inside a process) → AssemblyLoadContext.
.NET Remoting → gRPC and HTTP.
WCF server → gRPC or the community-run CoreWCF.
ASP.NET Web Forms → Razor Pages and Blazor.

WPF and WinForms came back in .NET Core 3.0, but only on Windows.

cards.q: One server needs apps on both .NET 8 and .NET 10. What is the problem?
options: None: versions install side by side, and each app uses its own
cards.explain: That is the difference from Framework, where 4.8 replaces 4.5.

cards.q: Match the old thing to its replacement
What can .NET Core do that Framework could not? Select all that apply.
options: Install several versions side by side
Ship the runtime together with the app
cards.explain: Core has no Web Forms.

cards.q: Does WPF on .NET 8 run on Linux?
options: No, WPF and WinForms in modern .NET are Windows-only
cards.explain: For cross-platform UI, there are Avalonia and MAUI.

lessons.title: .NET Standard
lessons.sub: An API contract, not a runtime. And why 2.1 matters

cards.title: A zoo of runtimes
cards.body:
By 2016 .NET came in several flavors: Framework, Core, Mono, Xamarin, Unity, UWP. Each had its own set of APIs.

Library authors did not know what to target. Build a separate DLL for each one?

cards.title: A standard is a list, not a program
cards.body:
.NET Standard is a list of APIs a platform must provide. It runs nothing by itself.

Think of a power outlet standard: it does not supply electricity, but any device with the right plug fits any outlet that follows the standard.

A library built for netstandard2.0 works anywhere .NET Standard 2.0 is implemented.

cards.q: What is .NET Standard?
options: A contract: a list of APIs a platform must implement
cards.explain: You cannot run an app "on .NET Standard". You can only build a library for it.

cards.title: 2.0 and 2.1
cards.body:
2.0 (2017) is a huge set, more than 30,000 APIs. It is implemented by Framework 4.6.1+ (reliably from 4.7.2), .NET Core 2.0+, Mono and Unity.

2.1 (2019) added Span<T>, IAsyncEnumerable and default interface methods. It is implemented by .NET Core 3.0+ and Unity 2021.2+. .NET Framework does not implement it. Its ceiling is 2.0.

cards.task: A teammate built a shared library for netstandard2.1. Make it work in both Revit 2024 and Unity with a single target.

cards.q: Why did Framework never get .NET Standard 2.1?
options: The new APIs need changes in the runtime itself, and Framework is frozen and updated in place
The license did not allow it
cards.explain: Default interface methods, for example, need CLR support. Changing a CLR that all of Windows shares is too risky.

cards.task: Shared code for Unity, Revit 2025 and a .NET 10 app. You need Span<T> and IAsyncEnumerable without extra packages. One target.

cards.title: The standard has stopped growing
cards.body:
There will be no .NET Standard after 2.1. Since .NET 5 there is just one platform, and a target like net8.0 or net10.0 means "everything in that version".

.NET Standard remains a bridge to Framework and Unity: 2.0 for maximum reach, 2.1 for Unity and modern .NET.

cards.q: Match each target to who can load it
pairs: Unity and modern .NET, but not Framework

cards.q: What is true? Select all that apply.
options: You can build an app for netstandard2.1 and run it
There will be no new .NET Standard versions
cards.explain: Only libraries are built for .NET Standard.

cards.title: TargetFrameworks, plural
cards.body: A project can build for several targets at once. You get several DLLs, and NuGet packs each one into its own folder in the package.

cards.title: Who gets which build
cards.body: Each consuming project takes the nearest compatible build. Given net8.0 and netstandard2.0, a .NET 10 app takes net8.0: it is closer and uses more features. Revit 2024 takes netstandard2.0.

cards.task: Revit 2025 should get a net8.0 build with the new APIs, while Revit 2024 and Unity keep working. Two targets at most.

cards.q: Targets are net8.0 and netstandard2.0. Which build does a .NET 10 app take?
cards.explain: net8.0 is compatible with .NET 10 and closer to it than the standard.

cards.title: Different code for different targets
cards.body: Where APIs differ, preprocessor symbols help. The SDK defines them for each target automatically.
cards.code:
#if NET8_0_OR_GREATER
    var hash = SHA256.HashData(bytes);           // new API
#else
    using var sha = SHA256.Create();
    var hash = sha.ComputeHash(bytes);           // works everywhere
#endif

cards.q: Code only for the .NET Framework build
cards.explain: NETFRAMEWORK is defined for net48 and other Framework targets.

cards.task: A plugin with separate code for Revit 2024 (net48) and Revit 2025 (net8.0), plus a shared part that must work in Unity.

cards.title: Revit plugins in practice
cards.body: A plugin for several Revit versions is usually one project with the targets net48 and net8.0-windows (the -windows suffix is needed for WPF). References to RevitAPI.dll are added conditionally, with the right version for each target.

cards.q: Match each symbol to when it is defined
Why bother with several targets if netstandard2.0 works everywhere?
options: To use newer, faster APIs on new platforms without losing the old ones
cards.explain: The standard itself is not slow. It just lacks the APIs that came later.

cards.task: One target that all four hosts load with no caveats.
All four hosts, but the .NET 10 app must get a net10.0 build and Unity must get netstandard2.1. Three targets at most.

cards.q: Why does .NET Standard 2.1 work in Unity and .NET 10 but not in .NET Framework?
options: Framework stopped at 2.0: the new APIs need runtime changes, and Framework is frozen
Unity and .NET 10 are the same runtime
cards.explain: Unity (Mono) and .NET 10 (CoreCLR) are different runtimes, but both implement 2.1.

cards.q: What came with .NET Core? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: AppDomain is exactly what was left behind.

cards.q: Build a library for .NET 8 and for Framework
cards.explain: Several targets mean TargetFrameworks, plural.

cards.q: Match each year to what happened
Targets are net48 and netstandard2.0. Which build does Revit 2024 take?
options: net48, since it is closer to Framework
cards.explain: NuGet picks the nearest target.

cards.q: What is .NET Standard, in one word?
cards.explain: It is a list of APIs. An actual runtime executes the code.

units.title: One .NET and where it is today
units.blurb: .NET 5-10, LTS and STS, what is new in .NET 10 and C# 14, where .NET runs today, and how Framework differs from modern .NET.

cards.title: 2020: just .NET
cards.body: After .NET Core 3.1 came .NET 5. The word "Core" was dropped: this is now the main .NET. Version 4 was skipped to avoid confusion with .NET Framework 4.x.

cards.task: Find the year .NET 5 came out.

cards.q: Why did .NET Core 3.1 jump straight to .NET 5 instead of 4?
options: Version 4 turned out to be buggy
cards.explain: ".NET 4" would have sounded like yet another Framework.

cards.title: A new version every November
cards.body:
Even-numbered versions are LTS (Long Term Support), supported for 3 years. Odd-numbered ones are STS (Standard Term Support): 2 years since .NET 9 (18 months before that).

.NET 8 (LTS) and .NET 9 (STS) lose support on the same day: November 10, 2026. .NET 10 (LTS) is supported until November 2028.

cards.q: It is October 2026, and your server runs .NET 8. What should you do?
options: Move to .NET 10 (LTS): .NET 8 support ends on November 10, 2026
cards.explain: Once support ends, security fixes stop coming.

cards.q: Match each version to its support type
What is true? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: .NET 5 continued .NET Core, not Framework.

cards.q: Target an app at the latest LTS
cards.explain: Since .NET 5, targets are named netN.0.

cards.q: Why is LTS a better fit for plugins and enterprise systems?
options: Longer support, so you upgrade the runtime less often
cards.explain: Autodesk and other big hosts move from one LTS to the next.

lessons.title: .NET 10 and C# 14
lessons.sub: What is actually new and what has been around for years

cards.title: .NET 10: the November 2025 LTS
cards.body:
The headline of every recent release is speed. The JIT removes more memory allocations and virtual calls, and libraries get Span<T>-based APIs that avoid extra copies.

And there is a new language version: C# 14.

cards.title: Not new, though people often think so
cards.body:
Nullable references: C# 8 (2019). On by default in project templates since .NET 6.
Records: C# 9 (2020).
Span<T>: 2018 (.NET Core 2.1 and C# 7.2).

None of these arrived in .NET 10. They just got easier to use and spread wider through the libraries.

cards.q: Match each feature to the C# version that introduced it

cards.title: C# 14: field
cards.body: Adding logic to a setter used to mean declaring a backing field by hand. Now field is the hidden backing field of an auto-property.

cards.title: C# 14: extension members and ?.=
cards.body:
An extension block adds not just methods but also properties to someone else's type.

Assignment through ?.: if the left side is null, nothing happens.

cards.q: A property that trims spaces, with no field of your own
cards.code: public string Name { get; set => ___ = value.Trim(); }
cards.explain: _name would work only if you declared that field yourself.

cards.title: Running a single file
cards.body: In .NET 10 you can run a one-file program with no project: dotnet run app.cs. Packages are pulled in by a directive right in the file. Handy for scripts and experiments.

cards.q: What does customer?.Order = GetOrder() do when customer is null?
options: Nothing: no assignment happens, and GetOrder() is not called
cards.explain: The right side is evaluated only if the left side is not null.

cards.q: What is actually new in C# 14 / .NET 10? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Records and nullable are old features, from C# 9 and C# 8.

cards.q: Where do you usually see the biggest win from moving to a new .NET without changing code?
options: Speed: the JIT and libraries get faster with every release
cards.explain: Many teams see a gain just by switching the target and rebuilding.

cards.title: The map in 2026
cards.body:
Servers and cloud: ASP.NET Core, on Linux and in containers.
Desktop: WPF and WinForms (Windows), Avalonia and MAUI (cross-platform).
Browser: Blazor on WebAssembly.
Games: Unity (Mono and IL2CPP, moving to CoreCLR), Godot 4 on .NET.
CAD and BIM: plugins for Revit, AutoCAD, Navisworks.

cards.title: Autodesk moved to .NET 8
cards.body:
Up to and including version 2024, Revit and AutoCAD ran on .NET Framework 4.8. Since 2025 they run on .NET 8.

So a plugin for both eras means two builds: net48 and net8.0-windows. Future host versions will follow new LTS releases. To learn the runtime of a specific version, check the "What's New" notes for its API.

cards.task: Find the year Revit and AutoCAD moved to .NET 8.
A plugin for Revit 2024 and Revit 2025: give each one its native build.

cards.q: Why can't a Revit 2025 plugin just stay on net48?
options: Revit 2025 runs on .NET 8. A Framework build might load with caveats at best and can crash on missing APIs
cards.explain: Autodesk explicitly requires plugins to be rebuilt for .NET 8.

cards.q: Match each task to a technology
Where does C# run today? Select all that apply.
cards.explain: Exactly what was missing in 2002.

cards.q: Godot 4 runs C# scripts on...
cards.explain: Godot 4 moved to modern .NET, unlike Godot 3, which used Mono.

lessons.title: Framework vs .NET: the differences
lessons.sub: A cheat sheet and a migration plan

cards.title: The key differences
cards.body:
Where it runs: Framework on Windows; .NET on Windows, Linux, macOS.
Installation: Framework is one per system, updated in place; .NET versions sit side by side or ship with the app.
Evolution: Framework gets fixes only; .NET gets a new version every year.
Speed: .NET is noticeably faster.

cards.title: Projects look different
cards.body: An old .csproj is hundreds of lines listing every file, plus packages.config. The new SDK style is a few lines: files are picked up automatically, and packages come via PackageReference.

cards.q: Which line gives away that this project targets .NET Framework?
cards.explain: SDK style works for Framework too. TargetFramework sets the target.

cards.q: Match: Framework → modern .NET

cards.title: How teams migrate
cards.body:
1. Convert projects to SDK style.
2. Move shared code into a netstandard2.0 library that works on both sides.
3. Find incompatible APIs (analyzers, .NET Upgrade Assistant).
4. Replace what is missing: WCF server, Remoting, Web Forms.
5. Switch the app to net10.0 and run the tests.

cards.q: Can you write C# 12 for net48?
options: Much of the syntax compiles, but only C# 7.3 is officially supported, and features that need new APIs or runtime support will not work
cards.explain: Default interface methods, for example, need runtime support, and Framework does not have it.

cards.q: Why .NET Standard 2.1 rather than 2.0 for code shared by Unity and .NET 10?
options: 2.1 has Span<T>, IAsyncEnumerable and default interface methods, and you do not need Framework here
2.0 is outdated and will not load
cards.explain: If you also need Framework, it is 2.0 or a separate net48 build.

cards.q: What is true in October 2026? Select all that apply.

cards.q: What is the takeaway from the whole story?
options: Code lives in the host's runtime: first find out where it will run, then pick the target
cards.explain: Revit, Unity and the server dictate the runtime. The TFM just answers them.
